analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from paying workers less for equivalent jobs because of sex, race, or national origin.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2026 with zero cosponsors, has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee with no action since the day it was referred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act so employers could not pay lower wages to jobs dominated by women or people of color when those jobs demand equivalent skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions to better-paid jobs. It would add compensatory and punitive damages for workers who win pay-discrimination cases, bar employers from retaliating against workers who discuss their wages, require larger employers to report pay by sex, race, and national origin to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and extend the same rules to congressional and executive branch employees. It would take effect one year after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and workers of color in traditionally female- or minority-dominated occupations, such as care work, cleaning, and clerical jobs, who could sue when their pay is lower than pay for different-but-equivalent jobs. The bill's findings estimate the existing wage gap costs American women roughly $500 billion a year in lost wages. Workers would also gain the right to discuss wages without retaliation and stronger remedies, including expert fees and class actions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and workers of color in undervalued jobs

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to pay equal wages for 'equivalent jobs' — different jobs whose combined skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions are the same — extending current equal-pay law beyond jobs that are substantially identical.
Adds compensatory and punitive damages, expert fees, and class-action treatment for pay-discrimination cases, on top of the back pay now available under the Equal Pay Act.

Makes it illegal for employers to fire, discipline, or intimidate workers who ask about, disclose, or compare wages, and for anyone to retaliate against workers who file or support a pay-discrimination complaint.

Requires employers with 25 or more employees (15 after the first two years) to report pay rates by sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC, which must protect employee confidentiality and may publish the data.
Applies the same equivalent-pay protections to congressional staff and executive branch employees, so the government is covered by the rules it sets.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found to be paying different wages for equivalent jobs would owe back pay, possible compensatory and punitive damages, and legal costs, and would bear new record-keeping and reporting obligations. Businesses argue the 'equivalent jobs' standard is hard to apply because it reaches beyond identical work, and compliance costs would fall most heavily on industries dominated by women and minority workers, such as health care and food service.

drawbacks.text: The equivalent-jobs standard asks courts and the EEOC to compare pay across very different occupations, which would require case-by-case judgments about how much skill, effort, and responsibility different jobs demand and could produce unpredictable litigation for employers.

Employers must document and disclose pay by race, sex, and national origin, a compliance burden that falls on businesses of 15 or more employees, though the bill directs the EEOC to simplify reports for small firms and to protect employee confidentiality.

The bill's own findings concede that only part of the measured wage gap is unexplained; most cited factors — occupation, experience, education, and region — would remain lawful under the bill's carve-outs for seniority, merit, production systems, and bona fide job-related factors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a legal route to challenge pay disparities between equivalent jobs, plus stronger remedies and protection for pay transparency — would go directly to workers who are paid less in jobs historically dominated by women or minorities. The costs are real but mostly administrative and litigation-related for employers, and the bill already carves out seniority, merit, output-based pay, and bona fide business factors while barring employers from fixing gaps by cutting anyone's wages. Whether the standard works fairly in practice depends heavily on EEOC guidelines that do not yet exist, since the agency must define which jobs count as 'dominated' without a fixed list.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2026 in the House on May 4, 2026, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce that same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee has not held a markup, reported the bill, or taken any action since the referral, and Congress remains in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost from the outcome — employers retain the current, narrower equal-pay rules and workers' pay remains governed by existing law while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill is still pending

for.name: Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Delegate, District of Columbia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor, placing it before the Education and Workforce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no member besides the sponsor has taken a position; no other House member signed on as a cosponsor.

industries.industry: U.S. employers subject to the Fair Labor Standards Act
industries.note: The bill would expose employers that pay lower wages in jobs dominated by women or minorities to back-pay liability plus compensatory and punitive damages, new record-keeping and pay-reporting duties, and class actions. Employers' interest in avoiding that liability runs against the workers whose wages would rise.

industries.industry: Health care, food service, and other industries with large female- or minority-dominated workforces
industries.note: These sectors would face the largest adjustment if they must equalize pay between, for example, predominantly male jobs and predominantly female jobs demanding equivalent effort and skill. The bill prohibits raising one group's pay by cutting another's, so employers could not simply shift the cost onto existing employees.
The bill would hand the EEOC new rulemaking authority over job-domination guidelines, pay reporting, inspections, and data publication, expanding its role in wage enforcement.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors three weeks after introduction and no committee action, the bill's realistic path is the one most private members' bills take: it will likely remain in committee unless the sponsor attracts support or pay-equity legislation gains momentum in the chamber. A divided House makes committee consideration of a wage-discrimination bill unlikely this session.
